pages.text:
*Ama's Stall Ledger, Night 58. Bowls sold: 33. Broths tested: 9. Broths thrown out: 8.*

We needed one more thing. The lane was full of noise and light, but one friend still stood outside, holding her nose politely. Hui-Ting could not eat here. Her grandmother was Buddhist, and on the fifteenth of the lunar month, and often other days, she ate only vegetables. No meat, no fish, no garlic, no onion, no scallion.

Ama sat on a plastic stool, her wrist in a white brace. She looked at the empty corner of the stall where the small gas burner lived.

"Go on, then," she said. She did not offer advice or help. She just looked at me, and then she said the words she always said, but this time they felt like permission. "Taste first. Talk later."

I filled a small aluminum pot with water. I dropped in dried shiitake mushrooms, a dark strip of kelp, and a chunk of white daikon. I turned the flame to low. The water began to bubble, just barely, like a secret being told very quietly.

Two hours passed. The lane got louder. The steam got thicker. I was ready to taste.
pages.image: Lin, an 11-year-old girl with black bangs and a green jacket, stands at a small gas stove in a night market stall, stirring a small aluminum pot while a small grandmother with silver curls and a wrist brace watches from a plastic stool.

pages.text:
Broth one was thin. It had the texture of weak tea and tasted like water that had completely forgotten it was supposed to be soup. I poured it down the drain.

Broth two was worse. I had boiled the kelp too hard, and now the liquid tasted exactly like the ocean, specifically like a fish had been napping in the sink. That went out, too.

Broth three was a disaster. It tasted like a swamp. I do not have a better word for it. It was muddy, brown, and deeply sad.

Ama tasted each one. She did not make a face. She just nodded.

"Almost," she said.

I wanted to groan. Then I wanted to hug her. "Almost" is a good word. It means you are not done. It means you are right on the edge.

My fingers were stained brown from the mushrooms I was slicing. My hair smelled like a soup pot. I sniffed my sleeve and exhaled slowly. I did not care. I was not scrubbing my hair three times a day. Not anymore.
pages.image: Lin, with orange-stained fingers and messy black hair, holds a spoon to her mouth and frowns at a small pot of murky brown liquid, while Ama, in a floral vest, stands behind her with a calm, patient smile.

pages.text:
Hui-Ting came over to taste, because she is honest to the bone. She took a sip of broth six and frowned immediately. "Too sweet," she said before I could even ask. For broth seven, she shrugged her shoulders and picked at the loose end of her braid. "Weird," she announced.

I looked at Jun. He was carrying trays of empty bowls, his spiky hair damp with sweat, and he leaned in with a spoon to try broth eight. He made a short, sharp sound, like a squeaky toy getting stuck in a zipper.

"This is the worst soup in the history of soup," he declared.

I laughed until my stomach hurt. I had to sit down on a plastic stool, which wobbled dangerously under my weight, and I nearly toppled over into the drain. Ama poked my shoulder with her braced hand.

"Laughing?" she asked.

"Just a little," I wheezed.

"It is not a little," she said firmly. "It is a lot."
pages.image: Jun, a skinny boy with spiky hair, grimaces at a spoon of soup while Lin, in a red-and-white apron, sits on a wobbling plastic stool, laughing so hard her eyes are closed and her face is red. All shop signs, banners and hanging boards are smooth plain solid-color cloth.

pages.text:
I stopped and set the spoon down, suddenly remembering Mr. Tsai’s abacus. He had told me the blend was like an orchestra, where you do not just add more instruments, but find the one that is missing.

What was missing? It was not salt or sugar. It was something round, dark, and slow.

I scanned the vegetables until my eyes landed on two ripe tomatoes and a cob of corn. Holding them over the flame, I let the skins char until they turned black, sweet, and smoky. Then I peeled them and dropped them into the pot.

Next, I reached into the wooden box for Ama’s eight-spice pouch. I remembered the rule for Hui-Ting: no onion, no garlic, and no scallion. Just star anise, cinnamon, and the others.

I dropped the pouch in, and the smell changed immediately. It was deep, warm, and grounded. It smelled like home, but different, like a new kind of home.

I waited while the water bubbled again. This time, it sounded different. It sounded like it was thinking.
pages.image: Lin holds a small cloth pouch of spices over a pot, with charred tomatoes and corn on the counter beside her, while steam rises in a thick, fragrant cloud around her hands.

pages.text:
Broth nine.

Ama took the spoon, but she did not eat. Instead, she closed her eyes and let the steam hit her face. The lane was quiet except for the water bubbling and Uncle Feng laughing far down the row. She held a single curl of tangerine peel in her hand, and when she finally opened her eyes, she dropped it into the pot.

She handed the spoon back to me.

I passed it to Hui-Ting. She took a sip and stopped chewing. Her eyebrows shot up, and her mouth hung open a little.

"It tastes like your stall," she whispered.

I looked at my notebook and started writing. Dried shiitake, kelp, and daikon. Charred tomato, corn, and the pouch. Then, in the margin next to the numbers, I added a small note: (or whatever the weather wants).

Holding the pen, I felt a warmth in my chest that had nothing to do with the soup.
pages.image: Hui-Ting, a tall girl with two long braids and glasses, holds a spoon to her lips with a wide-eyed expression of surprise, while Lin, in a green jacket, watches her with a bright, hopeful smile and a notebook in her other hand.
